confidence_note: Book text not available. Facts come from the Publishers Weekly review (half of customers in five years, employees in four and a half, investors in under a year; cause-and-effect between employee and customer loyalty), publisher copy and a reader summary for the finer numbers (10-30% of customers a year, employee turnover 15-25%), which is medium confidence. The old text's complaint percentages, 'iceberg' term and 8-10 versus 5 word-of-mouth numbers are not attributable to the book and were dropped. The figures describe the mid-1990s business climate and could not be independently checked.
facts: Reichheld, a director at Bain & Company, wrote the book; Publishers Weekly (1996) describes the idea of loyalty as old-fashioned, seemingly obvious, and overlooked amid rapid turnover in business.

Major companies replace about half their customers in five years, about half their employees in four (jacket) or four and a half (Publishers Weekly) years, and about half their investors in under a year.

A reader summary: a typical company loses 10% to 30% of its customers each year; employee turnover of 15% to 25% a year is common; about 40% of US employees stay two years or less; disloyalty reduces corporate performance by 25% to 50% or more.
Customer defection is one of the most revealing measures of business failure; the goal is zero defections.

Central thesis: a cause-and-effect relationship between employee loyalty and customer loyalty. Disloyal employees rarely build lasting relationships with customers, which take time; long-term employees add value through training, efficiency, customer selection, retention and referrals.

Core recommendation: loyalty-based management, actively retaining customers and targeting those likely to stay; State Farm and Toyota/Lexus are examples of companies that improved their bottom line through loyalty.
scene_details: half the customers gone in about five years
half the investors gone in under a year
defection as a yardstick of failure
tension: Companies count the customers they win; the book asks them to count the ones who leave.
opening_idea: Open with the three half-lives: customers five years, employees four and a half, investors under one.

lessons.idea: Count departures as carefully as arrivals; who leaves shows how you are doing.
lessons.anchor: Defection as a measure of business failure.
lessons.example: A small bakery that counts new faces but never notes which regulars stopped coming.

reflect_final: Which person who quietly drifted away from you or your work lately could tell you something useful about why?

use_cases.situation: The team celebrates a good month of sign-ups.
use_cases.move: Ask how many people left in the same month and whether anyone knows why.

use_cases.situation: A client or colleague has gone quiet.
use_cases.move: Say you noticed the silence and ask whether anything you did or didn't do is worth hearing about.

use_cases.situation: You run a small shop or side business and feel good about new customers.
use_cases.move: Note that Reichheld treats who leaves as a measure of how you are doing, and ask which regulars have stopped coming.

pocket_idea: Count who leaves as carefully as who arrives; every departure is a measure of how you are doing.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Reichheld's book says a big company replaces half its customers in about five years and half its investors in under one.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Reichheld argues companies should watch departures: major firms replace about half their customers in five years, employees in four and a half, investors in under a year; he treats defection as a measure of failure and loyalty of staff as the cause of loyal customers.
